headline: Bendigo Bank viewed as a range-bound income stock with 6% dividend yield plus franking credits, but lacking the credit creation advantages of the major banks.
reasoning: Bendigo reported net interest margin of 1.95%, up 7 basis points, cash earnings up 3% (in line with inflation), and cash return on equity of 8%. The Up neobank was a highlight with 1.3 million customers up 11% and business loans through Up up 56% year-on-year. The stock trades at 16-17x earnings versus NAB at ~2x price to book and CBA at 3-4x. Regional banks cannot use internal risk-weighted asset models like the five major banks, limiting their credit creation ability. One host would want the fully franked yield to exceed 10% before becoming interested; currently it is approximately 6% cash yield, or ~9% including franking.
quote: I would be valuing a business like this based on the dividend yield. Because the way I think about it, X growth, it's not going to grow fast. But what do you get from it? If it doesn't grow fast, you get income... I would trade it almost like an annuity style investment. Like I'm buying it for an income stream. And I would want that income stream with the franking credits included to be up 10%... It's got a dividend of 6%. Fully franked would be about 9%. So I'd probably want to see that tipping over 10 in order for me to start to interested in a business like this.

headline: Sanjee Narandran avoids Bendigo and Adelaide Bank citing weak returns, data disadvantage versus majors, and rising bad debt provisioning
reasoning: Narandran says Bendigo's return on equity is low at 4-7%, and unlike the big four it lacks sufficient customer data to accurately assess credit risk. He notes all banks are now provisioning for bad loans, a sign the environment is deteriorating. He is cautious about businesses with high debt exposures and would not invest in Bendigo, citing systemic concerns about the second-tier banks' resilience in a credit downturn.
quote: The problem with Bendigo and the same is for all of our banks. There's not a lot of growth in it. With Bendigo, again, the return on equity is pretty low, between 4% and 7%. The difference between them and the big four is they don't have as much data to assess risk like the big four do. CBA has just got so much data, so many clients, they're able to manage and accept the risk much more accurately than if you've only got a portion of that type of data. And now we're seeing all the banks provisioning for bad loans and bad debts.
